stem: In the code below, which names are the parameters of `mix_paint()`?

options.rationale: Parameters are the names written in the brackets of the `def` line.
These are the arguments: the values passed in the call, not the names in the definition.
These are function names. Parameters are the names inside the brackets of the `def` line.
This mixes both groups: `color` and `litres` are parameters, while `"blue"` and `2` are arguments.

explanation: A parameter is a name in the function definition, like a labelled empty box. An argument is the value in a call that fills the box. Here `def mix_paint(color, litres):` defines the parameters `color` and `litres`, and the call `mix_paint("blue", 2)` passes the arguments `"blue"` and `2`.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
def book_room(guests, nights=1, breakfast="no"):
    print(guests, nights, breakfast)

book_room(2)
book_room(3, breakfast="yes")
book_room(1, 4, "yes")

options.rationale: A keyword argument goes to the parameter it names, not to the next free position, so `"yes"` goes to `breakfast`.
Missing arguments take their defaults, the keyword argument overrides only `breakfast`, and the last call overrides both defaults by position.
The keyword argument `breakfast="yes"` overrides the default `"no"` for that call.
A parameter with a default never gets `None` by itself: when the argument is left out, its default value is used.

explanation: `book_room(2)` gives only `guests`, so `nights` and `breakfast` use their defaults: `2 1 no`. `book_room(3, breakfast="yes")` overrides just `breakfast` by keyword, so `nights` stays 1: `3 1 yes`. `book_room(1, 4, "yes")` passes all three by position: `1 4 yes`.

stem: What happens when you try to run this program?

    print(message, to)

print("Writing a card")
send_card(to="Mia", "Happy birthday")

options.text: It prints `Writing a card` and then `Happy birthday Mia`.
options.rationale: Python does not sort the arguments out for you: a positional argument must never follow a keyword argument.

options.text: It prints `Writing a card`, then stops with a `TypeError` when `send_card()` is called.
options.rationale: The problem is found while Python reads the code, not while it runs, so not even the first `print()` happens.

options.text: Nothing is printed: Python reports a `SyntaxError` before the program starts.
options.rationale: A positional argument after a keyword argument is a syntax error, so Python refuses to run any line of the file.

options.text: It prints `Writing a card` and then `Mia Happy birthday`.
options.rationale: The call is not valid at all, so nothing is matched to the parameters.

explanation: In a call, all positional arguments must come first, then the keyword arguments. `send_card(to="Mia", "Happy birthday")` breaks this rule, which is `SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument`. A syntax error is found before the program starts, so `Writing a card` is never printed.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
print("tea", "milk", sep="&", end="|")
print("bread")
print("jam", "butter", sep="")

options.rationale: `sep` goes between the values, `end` replaces the newline, so `bread` continues on the same line.
`end="|"` replaces the newline completely, so the next `print()` continues on the same line.
`sep` is only put between values, never after the last one.
Setting `sep` replaces the default space; it does not add to it, and `sep=""` means no space at all.

explanation: The first `print()` puts `&` between `tea` and `milk` and ends with `|` instead of a newline. So `bread` is printed right after it, followed by the usual newline. The last call uses an empty separator, so `jam` and `butter` are joined: `jambutter`.

    print(main, side, drink)

options.rationale: `"soup"` fills `main`, the keyword overrides `drink`, and `side` uses its default.
Keyword arguments may come in any order, and every parameter without a default gets a value.
`main` has no default, so leaving it out raises `TypeError` (missing 1 required positional argument).
A positional argument after a keyword argument is a `SyntaxError`.
The function has three parameters, so four arguments raise `TypeError` (takes from 1 to 3 positional arguments).
`"stew"` already fills `main` by position, so the keyword gives it a second value: `TypeError`.

explanation: A valid call gives every parameter without a default exactly one value, puts positional arguments before keyword arguments, and passes no more arguments than there are parameters. Only `plan_meal("soup", drink="juice")` and `plan_meal(side="rice", main="fish")` follow all these rules.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.rationale: The `end=", "` keeps the three numbers on one line, and `sep` has no effect on a single value, so `go` is printed as is.
`sep` goes between values only; it is not added after the last one.
`end=", "` only replaces the newline of the first three `print()` calls. The last call ends the line normally, but nothing starts a new line before `go`.
`sep="*"` is used in the last call only, and that call has a single value, so there is nothing to separate.

explanation: `end` is what `print()` writes after its values, here a comma and a space instead of a newline. `sep` is what goes between several values in one call. In `print("go", sep="*")` there is only one value, so `sep` changes nothing.
